title: Sukkot: the four kinds (Leviticus 23:40)
hookLine: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, which midrash reads as four kinds of people held together

cards: On a Sukkot morning, someone stands in a sukkah holding what looks like a strange bouquet. In the right hand, a tall, closed palm branch, bound with sprigs of green leaves.
In the left, a yellow fruit like a bumpy lemon, held so carefully you'd think it was glass. People pay real money for a perfect one.
They say a blessing, bring both hands together, and wave the whole bundle: forward, to the side, behind, up, down. Gently, so the leaves rustle.

teach.b: It all comes from one verse.

The Torah says that on the first day of the festival, "ye shall take you on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm-trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook," and rejoice.

The rabbis identified the four: the etrog, a citron, for the goodly fruit; the lulav, a young palm branch; hadasim, myrtle, whose leaves grow thick and overlapping; and aravot, willows that grow by water.
The whole bundle is often just called the lulav, after the tallest piece. Then the midrash asks: why these four?
It answers by taste and smell. The etrog has both, like people who have both learning and good deeds. The palm's fruit, the date, has taste but no smell: learning without deeds.
The myrtle has a lovely smell but no taste: good deeds without learning. And the willow has neither. What does God do with the willows?
Throw them away? No. Bind them all into one bundle, and each makes up for the others.
You can't do this mitzvah with three of the four.

teach.h: ALL FOUR, OR IT DOESN'T COUNT.
teach.b: Leave out the plain willow and the whole thing doesn't count. Then the waving.

Many wave toward all six directions: east, south, west, north, up and down. The Talmud explains it as waving to the One to whom every direction belongs, and as a way of holding back harmful winds and dews.
And Sukkot sits right before the rainy season, so the willows of the brook join a festival that prays for rain.

how: On each day of Sukkot except Shabbat, many Jews hold the lulav, myrtle and willow together with the etrog, say a blessing, and wave them in six directions, and carry them around the synagogue during the Hoshanot prayers.

o: a branch waved to welcome a new king
a palm branch bound with myrtle and willow
a wreath of leaves hung over the doorway

games.q: four kinds, four kinds of people — tap the pairs.
p: taste and smell: learning and deeds

s: the lulav can be waved with just the three best plants
all four kinds are needed; leave out the willow and it doesn't count.
the etrog is a kind of citron
the goodly fruit of the verse, as the rabbis identified it.
many wave the four kinds toward six directions
east, south, west, north, up and down.

games.q: you're binding the four kinds. the willow looks plain and droopy next to the others. what do you do?
o: leave it out; three is plenty.
bind it in with the others.
swap it for a second myrtle.
games.why: the midrash says God binds all four together so each makes up for the others. without the willow, the mitzvah doesn't count.

practice: Point slowly to six directions: ahead, to someone you look up to; to each side, the people beside you; behind, the people who came before; up; and down, to the ground that holds you.
Then bring your hands together, think of one person who feels like a willow, easy to leave out, and hold them in the bundle.

wordCard.voice: Lulav. A young palm branch, bound with myrtle and willow and held with the etrog: four kinds of plants, and four kinds of people, together.

orig.note: Hebrew: a young, closed palm branch; the name for the whole bundle of four kinds.

carryVoice: Your line: every kind together. Even the plain willow belongs in the bundle. See you tomorrow.
